newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Furry animal leg trap debate tops EU talks.
newsitem.headline: Furry animal leg trap debate tops EU talks.

text.p: Luxembourg will prod the European Union on Tuesday to back a deal with Canada and Russia on more humane standards for the leg-hold traps used to ensnare animals like wolves, beavers and otters for their fur.

But EU officials said agreement on the controversial issue might be blocked again at a meeting of EU foreign ministers, which will also tackle a blueprint for EU expansion to eastern Europe and Middle East peace.
"It is a pretty routine agenda, but the leg-hold trap issue is one that could go either way," said an EU official.
The EU has been at odds with Canada, Russia and the United States for years over differences regarding what constitutes a humane way of trapping and killing furry animals.
The 15-nation bloc passed a law in 1991 making it illegal from January 1995 for the EU to import any fur from animals caught in leg-hold traps or so-called "drowning traps".

The law was postponed for a year but has still never been implemented as the Commission -- the EU's executive -- persuaded member states that they faced a serious risk of World Trade Organisation action if they banned imports of trapped fur.
The European Parliament and some member states such as Britain, however, have been arguing for a stronger stance and are furious with what they see as delaying tactics by the Commission.
On Tuesday Luxembourg -- the current EU president -- will introduce a proposal by which the EU would agree to allow imports of fur from animals caught in traps that met agreed humane standards.
Under the proposal, in agreement with Canada, there would be a ban on all kinds of jaw-type leghold traps for seven of 12 Canadian species under consideration.
Use of such traps for the remaining five species would be outlawed from March 31, 2000, but only provided the deal is in place before October 1 this year.
Under the draft deal, ministers will consider Russia will ban the traps by December 31, 1999, as long as it gets financial help to do so.
Another kind of trap, called padded traps, whose main difference is that they carry rubber strips on their jaws, would still be allowed.
Luxembourg hopes such a deal will pressure the United States into coming on board, but Britain and France have been suggesting they will oppose the move.

Russia, Canada and the United States argue that trapping fur is a legitimate way of life for thousands of indigenous ethnic groups and a ban on their products is unacceptable extra-territorial trade legislation.
The foreign ministers' meeting will open with a traditional beginning of presidency debate during which Agenda 2000 -- the EU's enlargement plans -- is likely to feature.

Foreign Ministers have also invited their Israeli counterpart, David Levy, for a dinner meeting, and EU sources say Luxembourg officials are currently trying to persuade Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to attend as well.
Ministers will also discuss the situation in former Yugoslavia as well as an international donors' conference on Bosnian reconstruction to be held in Brussels on Wednesday and Thursday.
